utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Does the prosecution hear? Do my colleagues? Mr Blaskic, do you hear me? Do you hear me, Mr Blaskic? THE DEFENDANT (in interpretation): Good morning, Mr President. I hear you very well, thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Good morning, everybody. We will now resume our hearing, and I could ask the Registrar just to tell us what is this case, and to say where it was that we stopped. I believe you can refer to the reference of the case and give the floor to the prosecution. Would you give us the case, please? THE REGISTRAR (in interpretation): Your Honour, this is case number IT-94-14-PT, the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you. I give the floor to you, prosecution, to respond to the arguments of the defence, having to do with the second preliminary motion, failure to punish. I give you the floor, prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. The defence has submitted that the court should disregard the failure to punish provision in Article 7.3 of the Statute. It is the submission of the prosecution that the defence motion should be denied, because failure to punish liability does not infringe the nullum crimen principle and because individual criminal responsibility for failure to punish is an integral part of the well-established doctrine of command responsibility. The prosecution would emphasise the obvious, that this is an International Tribunal applying international criminal law, and that it has been created by the Security Council with a particular mandate, and the defence is submitting that the Tribunal should, in fact, disregard that mandate. It is the submission of the prosecution that the Tribunal most emphatically should apply all of the law in the Statute, and that there is, in fact, no sound reason whatsoever for disregarding Article 7.3, the failure to punish provision, and Article 7.3 of the Statute. International law consists of treaties, custom and the general principles of law recognised by civilised nations. The nullum crimen principle is not violated if an act or omission is, at the time it is committed, a criminal offence under applicable national law, or a criminal offence under any of the components of international law, custom applicable treaties or general principles of law. Further, it is not essential that the act or omission be classified as the same crime at both time of commission and time of prosecution. It is sufficient if the act or omission is a crime at the time of commission, and a crime at the time of prosecution. It is the submission of the prosecutor that personal criminal liability is imposed on a commander for his failure to punish subordinates by both customary law and applicable treaty law, although, strictly speaking, it is only necessary to establish such liability under either customary or applicable treaty law to comply with the nullum crimen principle. The doctrine of command responsibility, whereby commanders can be held criminally responsible for the acts of their subordinates in certain circumstances, is well-established in customary law. The doctrine has two aspects: first, a commander may be held liable for offences which he has ordered to be committed; and secondly, in certain circumstances a commander may be held liable for the actions of his subordinates where he fails to exercise his duty to control his subordinates. The judgments in the Yamashita case and that by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East clearly indicated that commanders are held responsible for their failure to carry out a wide-ranging duty to control their subordinates. This duty includes a requirement to take practicable measures to punish offending subordinates. As opposed to the view asserted by the defence, it is the submission of the prosecutor that existing case law does provide support for the application of failure to punish liability, and other sources of customary law, such as national military manuals, provide an additional basis for this assertion. The defence draws an artificial and inappropriate distinction between failure to punish as an abstract concept and the commander's duty to prevent the occurrence, or recurrence, of offences. In several cases, accused were convicted for failure to punish, and part of the rationale for failure to punish constituting an offence was that the commander, as part of his general duty to control his troops, had a duty to prevent the recurrence of offences. Punishment is intended to deter the commission of future offences. When, however, a commander is held culpable for failure to punish, he is held culpable for offences which have already occurred, not for future offences. As examples, in the High Command case, Field Marshal von Kuechler was held responsible for the illegal execution of Red Army soldiers, which occurred before and after he took up command, because reports of these executions were made to his headquarters after he took up command and he took no punitive action. In the Hostages case, General Dehner was held responsible for the unlawful killing of hostages and reprisal prisoners ordered by his subordinates, because he failed to punish these subordinates, and in the Tokyo trial, General Tojo was held responsible for the death of prisoners on the Batan death march, because he failed to punish subordinates who ordered the march. These are some cases which provide support for failure to punish liability. The prosecutor must emphasise, however, that the case law for any punishment of international crimes is relatively spartan. This is not the equivalent of a domestic jurisdiction, where we have thousands upon thousands of cases. The cases that we have are relatively few. They occur at great intervals. In fact, the defence had suggested that they could find no examples of an International Tribunal holding someone criminally responsible for failure to punish. The prosecution submits that we have provided these examples, but, if one argued that simple lack of cases was an adequate basis for deciding that one should never punish or should never prosecute something, one might also point out that, until this Tribunal was established, no court has ever prosecuted for a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions, but it is submitted that no one would ever suggest that grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions were not legitimate international crimes. National law of war manuals also constitute evidence of state practice and provide important national assessments of customary international law. Two leading national law war manuals dating back to the 1950s, those of the British and American armies, assert that commanders are personally liable for failure to punish. The more recent German manual and the 1988 Yugoslav Regulations contain similar provisions. The Yugoslav Regulations are of particular significance. They state in part: "The commander who knows that the violations of the laws of war took place and did not charge those responsible for the violations is personally responsible. In case he is not authorised to charge them and he did not report them to the authorised military commander, he would also be personally responsible." The defence read a portion of the Yugoslav Regulations. We have perhaps read a slightly different portion. It is, however, submitted that no one could read the portion that we have just read without coming to a conclusion that a commander under the Yugoslav Regulations could be held criminally responsible for failure to punish. Further, General Blaskic, as a former professional officer in the Yugoslav army, could be expected to be intimately familiar with this particular provision. It is submitted by the prosecutor that personal criminal liability is imposed on a commander for his failure to punish subordinates by customary international law. In addition, however, to customary law, the international law doctrine of command responsibility is applicable to conflicts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, as a result of treaty obligations, specifically as a result of the 1977 Geneva Protocol 1 additional to the Geneva Conventions of 12th August 1949. This protocol applied throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia throughout the conflict, and a number of articles in that protocol, specifically Articles 43, 86 and 87, all essentially to a degree codify the doctrine of command responsibility, and also incorporate a specific provision relating to criminal liability for failure to punish. The negotiating history of Article 87 in particular clearly indicates it was intended to elaborate upon the obligations referred to in Article 86 in so far as the appropriate superiors were also military commanders. Additional support for the position that Articles 86 and 87 assign criminal responsibility for failure to punish is found in the 1988 Yugoslav Regulations, which state in part: "The commander who knows that the violations of the law of war took place and did not charge those responsible for the violations is personally responsible." It is submitted that the prosecution has adequately and fully established that the failure to punish provision in Article 7.3 does not in any way violate the nullum crimen principle. Further, it is submitted by the prosecution that, as a matter of substantive policy, the Tribunal should apply the doctrine of failure to punish liability. The fundamental premise of the doctrine of command responsibility is that a commander has a duty to control his subordinates, and to take all practicable measures to ensure that they comply with international humanitarian law. The Tokyo trial in particular emphasises the need to have a system in place to ensure law compliance, and to ensure the continuous and efficient working of the system. If the commander does not have a duty to enforce the law when his subordinates commit violations, both the doctrine and the disciplinary system break down. The commander has a duty to punish in order to deter future potential violators. A failure to punish condones the offence. Discussing the trials of German war criminals after the Second World War, the defence suggests on several occasions that failure to punish was only an element of another crime; for instance, the failure to prevent the recurrence of crimes. However, a reading of the Secretary-General's report pursuant to Security Council Resolution 808 containing the Tribunal's Statute clearly shows that the object and purpose behind Article 7.3 is precisely to prevent the commission of further crimes and to deter future unlawful behaviour. In paragraph 57 of the report, it is stated that, while a commander should be held responsible for the crimes committed pursuant to an order given by him, he should also be held responsible for failure to prevent a crime or to deter the unlawful behaviour of his subordinates. This imputed responsibility, or criminal negligence, is engaged if the person in superior authority knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit, or had committed crimes, and yet failed to take the necessary and reasonable steps to prevent or repress the commission of such crimes, or to punish those who had committed them. A distinction between failure to punish and failure to prevent is artificial. The failure to punish and the failure to prevent recurrence of criminal behaviour are intricately connected and a failure to punish subordinates who have committed crimes would, in most circumstances, also constitute a failure to prevent future crimes, and a failure to control one's own forces, the overarching duty of the military commander. The defence has indicated its concern that the principle contained in Article 7.3 is in violation of some unidentified norm of customary international law. It is the submission of the prosecution that one of the organisations which is most concerned about the rights of the accused under all circumstances is Amnesty International. Amnesty International produced a report entitled "The International Criminal Court making the right choices" in January of 1997. I quote from page 69 of that Amnesty International report: "A superior who fails to take measures to punish crimes which the superior knows, or has reasons to know, the subordinate has committed will send a message that such crimes can be committed with impunity. A superior who fails to take measures to prevent such crimes may justly be held responsible for such crimes." Article 7.3 of the Statute clearly imposes criminal liability for failure to punish. The Tribunal should not hesitate to use this provision in appropriate circumstances. The prosecutor submits that the defence motion should be denied. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you, prosecution. I believe that I see Mr Hayman has gotten up without having first asked whether he might speak. I think he wants to speak now. Do you hear me, Mr Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do, I had to move my head set, your Honour. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): I thought that you were going to speak without even asking permission from the Trial Chamber, and I understand that you wanted to answer quickly in response, so we are according you the right to speak, which you have almost taken for yourself. I give you the floor, Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would not presume such a right, your Honour, but I am grateful that the Trial Chamber will indulge a few moments of response from me. The prosecutor has repeatedly stated that we, the defence, are urging the Trial Chamber to disregard the Statute of this Tribunal. He used that word at least seven or eight times, and I am surprised he would use that terminology. We make very clear in our papers that what we are seeking is a ruling that liability, based solely on a failure to punish subordinates by a commander who learns after the fact of offences of misconduct by his subordinates is outside the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. We are not asking the court to disregard anything. We are asking for a ruling on the issue of jurisdiction, which of course raises the question whether the Trial Chamber and the Tribunal is competent to rule on its own subject matter jurisdiction. That is the issue I thought the prosecution would raise, instead of obfuscating that issue by using the word "disregard" over and over and over again. In fact, this Tribunal is competent to rule on its own subject matter jurisdiction, and that has been made perfectly clear, first, by the appellate decision in the Tadic matter on the defence motion for interlocutory appeal on jurisdiction, and I need only direct the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 10 through 12 of that opinion. I think they speak perfectly clear to, for example -- they use the phrase that, in defining "jurisdiction", that it is a power to exercise the judicial function, namely, that the Tribunal has to have that power to scrutinise its own power to exercise the judicial function with respect to a particular situation and a particular offence. What was found beyond, or stated to be beyond the jurisdiction of this court in the separate opinion of the Honourable Judge Li in that matter was, as I understand that separate opinion, the authority of the Tribunal to examine the legality of the Security Council resolution establishing the Tribunal itself, which, if I understand that opinion correctly, found that that power did not reside, and held that that power did not reside in the Tribunal. A different question from the issue of whether subject matter jurisdiction over a particular asserted offence exists. So I add those comments in an attempt to clarify what exactly we are seeking with respect to this motion. The prosecutor has also again repeated their argument that customary international law includes national law, and he did say that. We do not dispute that the American and the British military manuals contain language that suggests that failure to punish liability could lie against a commander and could lie in the sense that the commander could be held responsible, as a principal, for the underlying offences. But that is clearly not the case in the military manual of the former Yugoslavia. I think that was made perfectly clear yesterday -- I hope so -- in my argument, and, if you compare paragraph 1 and paragraph 2 of section 21 of that military manual, it is perfectly clear that there is no liability for failure to punish as a principal in that manual and I point out, of course, that is the military manual that governed the terrain, at least at a prior period of time the terrain on which the accused was, and was found. We again maintain that there is no such liability in international conventions, and I went through, painstakingly, Articles 86 and 87 of Additional Protocol 1 yesterday. The prosecutor has not responded to my specific comments with respect to, for example, in Article 86, subsection 2, the fact that it is an explicit reference to acts or crimes that are being committed, or about to be committed. There is absolutely no reference in Article 86 to past events. The prosecutor also cites to Article 43 of the Additional Protocol 1. Article 43 simply states that Armed Forces of a party shall have an internal disciplinary system. That is all. I do not know how the prosecutor can assert that Article 43 creates liability for failure to punish on the part of a commander based solely on acts the commander learned of after the fact. Then the prosecutor again cites to several case law instances, that is past cases of past Tribunal's decisions, and again asserts that they stand for the proposition that failure to punish liability shall exist as a separate and distinct offence, standing alone from failure to prevent. We have described each of the opinions he referenced in our briefs, and they most clearly do not stand for the proposition that failure to punish liability exists as a separate and distinct offence from failure to punish. Not to repeat what we have already said, we distinguish and describe the von Kuechler case at page 7 of our reply brief, the Tojo case at page 7, footnote 6, of our brief, and the Hostages case, involving General Dehner at page 5 of our reply brief. It is perfectly clear from those opinions none of them support failure to punish liability as a distinct offence, standing alone and apart from liability for failure to prevent. Now, I have to admit some perplexity on my part with the fact that the prosecutor continues to state that it is an artificial distinction between the offence of failure to punish and the offence of failure to prevent. Succinctly put, how can a distinction be artificial if it is between liability for past acts, with which you had no knowledge and your conduct has no causal connection, versus future acts that you have the ability and the power to prevent, and yet you failed to do so? Is that an artificial distinction? I think we all know, again, by our own internal barometers that that distinction is hardly artificial. Lastly, the prosecutor spoke of an Amnesty International quotation that I am not familiar with. I have not seen it. It was not in their brief, if I recall correctly. From the quote he read it was not clear to me that it supported failure to punish liability distinct from failure to prevent, but I will seek to obtain a copy of that after the hearing, and, if I have further comments on that citation, I will submit it to the Trial Chamber. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Would the prosecutor like to respond? At some point the Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber, with his colleagues, will have to put an end to this. But before putting the floor to the prosecutor, I would like to turn to Mr Hayman. Do you hear me, Mr Hayman, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): If you do not mind, I will ask you to read something. If you do not mind, could you reread paragraph 5.7 of the indictment, because it is at this point where there is most dispute? Many of these notions revolve around the fact that the acts were in the past, or that they will be in the future a distinction between them that one cannot punish somebody for future acts. Could you perhaps reread this? We all have it in front of us. That is paragraph 5.7 of the indictment, about which you were asking the Trial Chamber to withdraw. Do you have it at hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Could you reread it, please, slowly, calmly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In its entirety? JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Yes, the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: 5.7? JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): 5.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "The accused is also, or alternatively, criminally responsible as a superior for the acts of his subordinates pursuant to Article 7, section 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal. This criminal responsibility involves the responsibility of a superior officer for the acts of his subordinate, if the superior knew, or had reason to know, that his subordinate was about to commit such acts, or had done so, and the superior failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such further acts, or to punish the perpetrators thereof." JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): I will give the floor to the prosecutor. It somewhat bothers me to give the prosecutor the last word. I believe that the Presiding Judge has the responsibility in order to balance out the discussions, I think that we are all trying to do. Perhaps some brief observations on the part of the prosecution. If Mr Hayman, as I believe, wants to respond once again, I will ask him very briefly, otherwise I will stop. I will also ask the prosecutor to respond briefly, but even more briefly on the side of the defence. After that, we will put an end to this. So would you please respond, prosecution, but briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I shall be very brief, your Honour. First of all, at no time did the prosecution assert that customary law included international law. Essentially what we were doing was referring to the nullum crimen principle, which is quoted in Article 15 of the UN covenant on civil and political rights, and that states: "No one shall be held guilty of any criminal offence on account of any act or omission which did not constitute a criminal offence under national or international law at the time when it was committed." Secondly, the submission of the prosecutor is not that failure to punish is an offence all by itself. Failure to punish is a form of individual criminal responsibility, and Article 7 of the Statute of course refers to individual criminal responsibility. It does not refer to offences, and, thirdly, clearly, if there was, in fact, no atrocity committed, if no particularly serious act had ever occurred, of course the accused would not be charged with failure to punish -- I withdraw that -- would not be charged in relation to Article 7.3 of the Statute. There must be an offence to which Article 7.3 is linked. That is it, thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Prosecution, now, do we agree, so that everything will be transparent here, that in your mind, failure to punish must always be related, as it says in the Statute, to a crime or to a defence which was allegedly committed, and, therefore, you will have to prove this during the trial? Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, we do. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you. Very briefly, Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will close, your Honours, with the repeated observation that the indictment charges the accused with committing a plethora of acts and then having four -- at least three different mental states. That is in paragraph 5.7, namely, that under 5.6, he planned, instigated, ordered and aided and abetted, but then alternatively in 5.7, that he either knew or had reason to know that these offences were about to be committed, and he did not prevent them, or, alternatively, he learned they had been committed, and he failed to punish. Those are three different mens rea requirements: firstly, just to repeat again to make it perfectly clear, if I am not speaking clearly this morning, that he planned, instigated, ordered and aided and abetted them, that is in paragraph 5.6; secondly, that he knew or had reason to know that the acts were about to be committed, and he did not take reasonable measures to prevent them; or thirdly, that he learned his subordinates had committed the acts, and he failed to punish them. Those are three different mental states that they have alleged in the alternative as separate and complete mens rea states under the indictment, and under the Statute of the Tribunal. So when the prosecutor states that they do not take the position that failure to punish is a crime unto itself, let us make it perfectly clear that they take the position in the indictment -- and they have charged this man -- with, among other things, the offence of being responsible for everything in the indictment, all of the wrongful acts charged, based, in addition to other things, solely on his failure to punish acts about which he learned after the fact. They have charged that, those acts and that mens rea, as a crime unto itself. No other Tribunal has ever done that. If the court looks at these cases, no Tribunal has ever convicted anyone in history for that offence, and we submit this should not be the first Tribunal to do so, and, in fact, this accused should not be put through a trial on that charge. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you. The Trial Chamber would now like to hear both the parties on the third preliminary motion, that is mens rea required for command responsibility. You do understand, Mr Hayman, I do want to tell you this, if you do hear me, that a certain number of your preliminary motions, there is a mixture of what would be a motion on lack of jurisdiction, or on defects in the form, and in some of the motions on lack of competence, there is also a movement from one to the other. If I am saying this to you, it is not in order to reproach you for anything. You are organising General Blaskic's defence as you like, but this is simply in order to encourage you to be clear in what constitutes one motion as opposed to another for the Trial Chamber, of course, as well as the prosecutor, so that we will be able to know whether we are talking about, one preliminary motion or the other. Because you say you have just completed your argument now on the previous motion speaking about command responsibility, and now we are going to go into the third motion, which, in fact, deals with command responsibility. So now would you please argue to that motion, or Mr Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. This motion is related to the last motion just argued in the sense that, by this motion, the accused seeks to know, after eleven months of incarceration awaiting trial, by what general mens rea standard he will be judged at trial. He does not know that, as he sits here today. That is all we seek, but we seek no less than to know the standard, the mental standard, the intense standard by which he will be judged at trial. In their papers, the prosecution concedes that the applicable mens rea standard is "essential to the outcome of the trial". That appears in their response at page 7. Yet they also argue that this Trial Chamber cannot address this issue, because they lack a right of interlocutory appeal, should the Trial Chamber rule in some manner unsatisfactory to the prosecution. They also argue that the Trial Chamber should not address this issue at this time, because the defendant has no need to know the mens rea standard applicable to command responsibility before, or, it appears, even during the trial. Apparently, the prosecution believes that the parties need only know the standard of conduct, that is the mens rea standard applicable to command responsibility, at the time final judgment is rendered. Of course, by then, at that late juncture, it will be too late, it will be too late at that point to elicit all the testimony relevant to the specific standard, mens rea standard, governing this case, that this Trial Chamber finds appropriate to govern the case, to make all appropriate legal and factual arguments relevant to the mens rea standard that the Trial Chamber finds applicable, because, of course, the trial will be over. First, if I may look at their argument and respond to their argument, that, because there is a lack of a right of interlocutory appeal on the part of the prosecution, that the Trial Chamber is in some way incompetent to address this issue. This is, in a sense, prefatory, the two questions proposed by this motion I think are the merits, what is the mens rea applicable and then, secondly, procedurally is this the right time for the Trial Chamber to address this issue? So first, if I may, I will address whether this is the right time to address the issue. The prosecution's argument that the Trial Chamber is not competent to address this issue, because it lacks a right of interlocutory appeal, if taken to its logical conclusion, would result in the following: imagine that the trial is concluded, that is the evidence has been received, all evidence is finished, it is the time for final argument of counsel, and the defence asks to know what is the mens rea standard before the court recesses for deliberations. The prosecution could still object that the Trial Chamber should not articulate a mens rea standard, because at that point in time the prosecution would not have a right of interlocutory appeal if the Trial Chamber said that the applicable mens rea was strict liability, or whatever. The only right of appeal that either party would have concerning the Trial Chamber's articulation of what the appropriate mens rea standard is is an appeal from the final judgment. So, in that sense, the prosecution's argument is that the court should not address this issue, because they lack a right of interlocutory appeal, it proves too much, and thus it proves nothing. Now, secondly, they argue, the prosecution argues, that the defendant does not need to know what the mental standard is governing command responsibility, and here, of course, we are talking about the know, or reason to know requirement of Article 7, section 3 of the Tribunal's Statute, specifically -- really both of them, they are both implicated in this discussion. The prosecution argues that the meaning of these two phrases, to know, and reason to know, is self-evident, and no further articulation of what that means is necessary from the Trial Chamber. Yet I think the divergence of opinions, and positions articulated by the defence and the prosecution on this issue, disproves their own argument. They argue in their papers that command responsibility creates a responsibility for the commander with respect to the conduct of the members of other Armed Forces on the terrain, and, in fact, of the local population -- that appears in their response at page 17. They argue that certain facts, such as the widespread nature of offences standing alone, should create a presumption of knowledge on the part of the defendant. Very extreme positions, I would submit. We vigorously contest these and other assertions, but what they certainly do is they highlight the absolute need of the parties to know the applicable mens rea standard before trial. How can the defence try this case competently, not knowing whether our client is going to be held to a strict liability standard, or, on the other hand, perhaps held to the standard of wanton and immoral disregard of facts actually within his possession as urged in our papers? Now, if I may, I will turn to the merits, and to what that standard, the mens rea standard for command responsibility liability, in our view, should be. First, I note there is some area of agreement between the parties, at least with respect to the reason to know portion of Article 7, section 3. The prosecution appears to concur that the mens rea standard under the reason to know element must be based on wanton and immoral disregard of certain facts. That is in their papers. They are not seeking a strict liability standard under the reason to know element. They are not seeking a negligence standard. They are not seeking a gross negligence standard. Rather, they concur that a wanton and immoral disregard of certain facts standard, or framework, is appropriate. That is where the agreement between the parties ends. We disagree as to the rest of this standard, namely, wanton and immoral disregard of what? Our position is as stated in our papers, that command responsibility liability under the reason to know element should only lie where there is wanton and immoral disregard of facts actually in the possession of the commander, compelling the conclusion that offences are being committed, or are about to be committed. That is the standard we seek. The prosecution seeks a different and much more lenient, much more far-reaching standard. They do concede, however, that the reason to know element of Article 7, section 3 is taken from Article 86, subsection 2 of Protocol 1 Additional to the 1949 Geneva Convention, and that is, we maintain, quite instructive, because, if one looks to Article 86, subsection 2 of Protocol 1 Additional, one sees that the standard in that article is both objective and subjective, but the first portion is objective, because Article 86, subsection 2 requires that the commander actually have information. Let me take a moment, if I may, and put my fingers on that section, so I can read from it. I will quote it from memory and if I misstate it, I am sure the prosecution will correct me. The standard in Article 86, subsection 2 is not a "should have known" standard. It is a "reason to know" standard, and the commentary and delegate's comments concerning the adoption of Additional Protocol 1 make perfectly clear that an objective standard was intended, not a subjective standard, not a "should have known" standard, not a negligence standard. We further maintain that the information that the prosecution should have to demonstrate was in the possession of a commander, so that a commander had reason to know, and knowledge, that offences were either being committed, or were going to be committed, that information should be specific, and it should be shown to actually be in the commander's possession, because we fear that the mens rea standard becomes subjective. It becomes a "should have known" standard, and quickly degenerates into a standard of negligence. The prosecution also argues that a presumption of actual knowledge -- now I am turning to the first component or element of Article 7, section 3. That is actual knowledge. That is a commander who knew acts were being committed, or were about to be committed and allegedly failed to prevent their commission. Here the prosecution seeks an evidentiary presumption of actual knowledge, where crimes of subordinates are widespread. Having agreed under the reason to know standard that wanton and immoral disregard is the appropriate standard, the prosecution attempts, under the actual knowledge prong of Article 7, section 3, to revive a strict liability standard, that some find support for in the Yamashita case. That position, though, of course, has been universally discredited. It is also fundamentally at odds, the idea of a presumption of actual knowledge arising from the mere existence of certain facts, such as widespread offences, it is fundamentally at odds with the presumption of innocence in Article 14 of the UN Convention on civil and political rights, and we submit it is also fundamentally at odds with the principle in dubio poraio, or the prosecution's burden to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. In fact, a prosecutor fifty years ago sought a presumption of exactly this sort in the High Command case after World War 2, and one need only look to the High Command case for the specific rejection of a prosecutor's request for an evidentiary presumption of this nature, and we cite the location in that opinion in our brief, where that rejection can be found. Lastly, we submit that the mens rea standard sought by the prosecution conflicts with modern concepts of personal guilt, personal responsibility. Those concepts were discussed yesterday by my colleague, Mr Nobilo, and I think they have application here, as well as to the prior motion, but they need not be repeated. So, in summary, we not only believe that this is a very serious issue on the merits, where there is significant disagreement between the parties and the prosecution has taken extreme positions, we believe, but it is also an issue that cries out for a ruling before trial, so that we can proceed efficiently through trial, eliciting the specific testimony and evidence that is relevant to the standard by which our client will be judged, and so that the accused and the defence, and the prosecution, can have the benefit of knowing what that standard is, so we can prepare more effectively, present more effectively, and argue more effectively, and ultimately represent our client more effectively before this Trial Chamber. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Thank you, Mr Hayman. Mr Prosecutor, do you have a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr President. The prosecutor submits, first, that the defence motion should be denied as it relates to a matter which is not appropriate for a preliminary motion. There is no question as to the competence of the court. The question, in fact, from the point of view of the prosecutor, has to do with whether or not the court might wish to exercise its discretion to consider this particular motion. The defence motion seeks a ruling on fundamental questions of substantive law relating to the culpability of the accused. It is the submission of the prosecutor that the Trial Chamber should not make such a ruling at this time, because, first, the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber to date indicates that there may be no right of interlocutory appeal on this matter. Secondly, it is conceivable that, if a ruling was, in fact, erroneous, not that we would be suggesting that it would be, but, if it was, it might end up constituting some sort of a precedent in future cases. But, most of all, the prosecution submits that now is not the right time to make a ruling on this particular issue. If we review the existing cases, as the defence of course does so, as do we, when we are looking at a later portion of our respective briefs, it is clear that, when one descends from the general to the particular, when one tries to elaborate on the mens rea of this type of issue, one must pay considerable heed to the facts. Different cases produce different verbal formulations of what the standards are. If, for example, one looks at the German cases, by and large what we have there is a set of circumstances where the court is able to consider elaboration of documentary evidence, where it appears to have a number of witnesses who were intimately involved in the decision-making process, where we have what has been referred to as a German penchant for meticulous record-keeping. On the other hand, there tends to be a different type of verbal formulation for the mens rea, when we are looking at the cases involving Japanese defendants at the end of the Second World War, because the paper trail is not anywhere -- is not kept in such detail. There are no meticulous records, or at least there does not appear to be access to meticulous records. There does not appear to be a possibility of putting the same range of witnesses on the stand to testify as to the inner aspects of the decision-making process. In other words, it is the submission of the prosecution that it is most appropriate for it to elaborate on the actual content of mens rea at a point in time when it has, in fact, the vast bulk of the evidence before it, when it knows precisely what it is that it must come to a decision on, and at this present stage, it is preferable to retain a high level of generality concerning any statement related to mens rea for command responsibility, and that, in fact, the expression "knew or had reason to know" provides adequate guidance for the defence at this time in preparing its defence. If, however, the chamber wishes to address the specific issue of mens rea related to Article 7.3, then of course the prosecution has a number of observations which it submits should be taken into account. It is the submission of the prosecutor that, in view of the characteristics of the doctrine of command responsibility, and its peculiarity to international law, the mens rea standard can be properly appreciated only in the broader context of the far-reaching and comprehensive duty of military commanders, who take all necessary measures to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law on the part of their subordinates. Article 7.3 of the Statute codifies a well-established norm of international customary and treaty law concerning the criminal liability of superiors for the actions of their subordinates. Specifically, it is submitted that Article 7.3 represents or reflects a species of accomplice liability, peculiar to international law, which clarifies the scope of Article 7.1 as it relates to persons in a position of superior authority. If, for example, one goes back and explores the roots, how this particular doctrine evolved, certainly none of the chambers which considered command responsibility and which developed the doctrine at the end of the Second World War had some kind of statutory provision which referred specifically to the doctrine of command responsibility. What they did, what those tribunals did, was develop the general concept of criminal participation of parties to criminal offences, and adapt it to the specific circumstances of the military commander. With respect to the term "knew" under Article 7.3 of the Statute, the prosecutor agrees in part with the contention of the defence that actual knowledge established by direct evidence is conceptually similar to actual knowledge established by circumstantial evidence, and that the latter is not necessarily a conceptually distinct form of mens rea. However, it is submitted by the prosecutor that the separate listing of actual knowledge established by circumstantial evidence, or what is frequently referred to as the "must have known" standard, is desirable because the concept is so distinct in evidentiary terms. In particular, where the necessarily circumstantial evidence consists of crimes of public notoriety, or of crimes committed on a large scale or widespread or systematic basis, there is a presumption, admittedly a rebuttable presumption, but nevertheless a presumption of authorisation, or encouragement, or connivance or acquiescence on the part of the individual commander. I would like now to turn to the "had reason to know" provision in Article 7.3. The defence argues that the "had reason to know" provision should be defined as "wanton disregard of objective facts within the accused's actual possession, compelling the conclusion that the accused's subordinates were about to commit, or had committed, the criminal acts alleged in the indictment." It is the submission of the prosecution that, although this formulation by the defence certainly falls comfortably within the ambit of "had reason to know", in fact, a substantially broader approach should be taken when one is attempting to define mens rea in relation to "had reason to know." With respect to the "had reason to know" standard, the prosecutor submits that a military commander bears criminal liability for wanton disregard, not only of objective facts within his actual possession, as the defence motion suggests, but also of facts which are not within his actual possession, by reason of a personal dereliction on his part to properly supervise his subordinates, and, in particular, to require and obtain adequate reports, or information, and to be apprised of the actions of his subordinates. Under international law, a military commander bears an affirmative, not a passive duty, to be apprised of occurrences within his area of operations. A military commander is not the average citizen in an average set of circumstances. He is a person who bears a high degree of responsibility for controlling his troops, and it is only in that light that the mens rea for the doctrine of command responsibility can be properly assessed. Support for the prosecution position is, it is submitted, found in the Yamashita case, the hostages case, and the decision of the international military Tribunal for the Far East. It is in light of this well-established jurisprudence that the standard of "had reason to know" in Article 7.3 of the Statute, and the substantially identical standard of "had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time", which is contained in Article 86.2 of Protocol 1, should be considered, and one might elaborate slightly further. The international law commission, in its commentary on the draft code of crimes against the peace and security of mankind, indicated, first of all, that the Protocol 1 standard and the standard in our Statute were essentially identical, and then went on to conclude that the "had information enabling them to conclude" standard of Protocol 1 simply means that the superior has sufficient relevant information to enable him to conclude, under the circumstances at the time, that his subordinates are committing, or are about to commit a crime. In this situation, a superior does not have actual knowledge of the unlawful conduct being planned, or perpetrated by his subordinates, but he has sufficient relevant information of a general nature that would enable him to conclude that this is the case. With respect to the affirmative duty to know, the international law commission states: "A superior who simply ignores information which clearly indicates the likelihood of criminal conduct on the part of his subordinates is seriously negligent in failing to perform his duty to prevent or suppress such conduct by failing to make a reasonable effort to obtain the necessary information that will enable him to take appropriate action." The prosecution is not arguing that a strict liability standard is appropriate. In fact, we agree whole-heartedly with the defence that a strict liability standard is not appropriate. On the other hand, one must bear in mind the very substantial duties, positive duties imposed on a military commander in determining what is the appropriate mens rea for Article 7.3 of our Statute. It is the submission of the prosecutor that the Tribunal should establish the requisite mens rea under Article 7.3 as follows: first, actual knowledge established through direct evidence. It would be submitted that the defence would clearly agree with that standard also. Second, actual knowledge established through circumstantial evidence. In this respect, it is submitted that that formulation would probably be acceptable to the defence. However, the prosecution would go on and suggest that there should also be a rebuttable presumption of actual knowledge obtained through circumstantial evidence, where the crimes of subordinates are a matter of public notoriety, are numerous, occur over a prolonged period, or in a wide geographic area. Then the third aspect of mens rea, in other words, in circumstances where one cannot establish actual knowledge, then we would have a standard of wanton disregard, using, I believe, an expression used by the defence, but a broader expression of that, wanton disregard of information of a general nature, within the reasonable access of a commander, indicating the likelihood of actual or prospective criminal conduct on the part of his subordinates. It is submitted that this particular formulation of the criterion is substantially similar to that already adopted by the International Law Commission. The defence goes on, and on the basis of its formulation of the mens rea under Article 7.3, it submits that it is necessary for the prosecution to provide an additional bill of particulars concerning the time of the commander's actual knowledge, or wanton disregard of facts in his possession. In particular, it is a contention of the defence that, as a matter of international customary law, the prosecutor must demonstrate the specific timeframe within which the commander allegedly acquired his mental state, as well as the objective facts actually within the accused's possession that compelled the conclusion that such acts were being committed, or were about to be committed. Both of these elements relate to the knowledge of the accused about the acts of his subordinates within the ambit of Article 7.3. It is the submission of the prosecutor that the appropriate standard to be applied in this respect is contained in the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and not in customary law, that, according to this standard, the prosecutor is obliged to submit only such particulars as may be necessary in order for the accused to prepare his defence, and to avoid prejudicial surprise, and that, in addition to the supporting material which has already been submitted to the accused, the indictment itself already contains sufficient particulars with respect to the knowledge of the accused under Article 7.3 as required by the standards contained in the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Contrary to the assertion in the defence motion, customary international law simply does not contain a clear standard with respect to bills of particulars, let alone specific requirements for an indictment based on the doctrine of command responsibility. The reference in the defence motion to the requirement imposed by the US Military Tribunal in the high command case to the effect that the time of knowledge must be established relates to establishing the guilt of the defendant at trial, and not to a bill of particulars. The Chamber might also wish to note that the defence has already received two statements of fact, with respect to both the original and amended indictments, a memorandum on jurisdiction attached to the original indictment, and over 3,500 pages of supporting material, including over 120 witness statements under Rule 66A. It is submitted that the present indictment is consistent with the standards contained in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and the prosecutor requests that the defence motion with reference to a bill of particulars also be denied. In conclusion, and in totality, the prosecution respectfully submits that the defence motion should be denied. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Hayman, I assume that you would like to respond, but I suggest that we suspend the meeting and meet again at 11.45. Do not worry, you will have much more time to prepare yourself. The meeting is adjourned until 11.45. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.45 am) JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Hayman, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I think I have four points to make in response to the prosecutor's arguments. First, the phrase in Article 86, section 2 of Protocol 1 Additional that I was attempting to recall, is set forth at page 15 of the defence motion concerning mens rea, and the specific phrase is -- let me read a larger phrase and then call your attention to the phrase I wish to highlight, and that is: "This Article provides the fact that a breach of the conventions or of this protocol that was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superiors from penal or disciplinary responsibility, as the case may be, if they knew, or had information", so the first phrase I would like to call your attention to is the phrase "had information", and that is a reference to an objective standard that the commander actually possessed information, and it is on this Article of Protocol 1 Additional that Article 7, subsection 3 -- JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Just a moment, please. We have just been told that the public gallery is not hearing. Since this is a public hearing, unless such time should come that the Trial Chamber feels it should not be -- excuse me, Mr Hayman. Does everybody else hear? Does the prosecution hear? Mr Blaskic, do you hear? Then it is simply the public gallery. Can this be fixed immediately? Do you hear me now in the gallery? All right, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So the fact that in Article 86, subsection 2 the phrase "had information" is used clearly indicates, and the delegates that were involved in the adoption of this Article discuss this fact, and, in fact, certain delegates as cited in our papers expressly condition their approval of this Article on the fact that the standard was objective, not subjective, with respect to the information being in the possession of the commander. We feel that is very important, and it certainly should bear on the interpretation of Article 7, subsection 3, with respect to the reason to know element, or standard. That is reason to know should not be "should have known". It is not equivalent to "should have known". It is equivalent to a standard whereby the commander actually possesses information. Then, secondly, Article 86, subsection 2 continues: "Or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time that the subordinate was committing, or was going to commit a breach." So, on top of this objective requirement that the commander actually possessed information, there is a subjective requirement that, from that information, it should have been concluded that a crime was being committed, or was going to be committed, and that is what we base our additional request on, that the mens rea standard should encompass the fact that the objective facts known to the commander should compel the conclusion that crimes are being committed, or will be committed in the future. Turning more directly to the prosecutor's responsive arguments, first, again, with respect to the process, whether this is an appropriate issue to be submitted to the Trial Chamber and decided at this time, the defence concedes that, in many cases, it would be unusual for the Trial Chamber to be called upon to articulate an important legal standard governing the case. If you imagine a case of murder or bank robbery -- we have many bank robberies in my country -- or other types of routine offences, there is no need for the trial court in those cases to articulate the legal standard in advance of the trial. The legal standards, the elements of the offences, are set forth in books, in many cases they have not changed in years. They are there for everyone to see. So we concede this is unusual, but this is not the usual case. The legal standard governing this case, governing the command responsibility charges and allegations made by the prosecution, they do not appear in a manual of law governing a court or a jury. In fact, no court has articulated this standard in fifty years. So this is an exceptional case. This is an historic case, and the defence believes that, although unusual, it is entirely appropriate here that the Trial Chamber be called upon to articulate the legal standard that will govern the core issue of this case. That is what mens rea is applicable to a charge of command responsibility. Now, the prosecutor has further stated that the formulation of a crime will differ, and the formulation of command responsibility as a crime in the mens rea associated therewith will differ according to the facts and circumstances, and thus there is a different formulation for the German army, a different formulation for the Japanese army, and so forth. That is hardly reassuring for the defence. We are not suggesting this is an easy task, to articulate the legal standard, but we believe it is necessary. We believe this is an obligation of the Trial Chamber. It is an historic occasion, and because of the historical nature of the occasion, the Trial Chamber should articulate the standard, and there are sound and important reasons for it. Now turning to the merits, again the prosecutor has suggested that, based on certain facts, such as the widespread nature of offences by subordinates, a rebuttable presumption that the accused encouraged, acquiesced, perhaps even was more active in causing the offences to occur should lie. I noted in my earlier argument that the High Command Tribunal explicitly rejected this type of presumption, and I would simply like to call the Trial Chamber's attention to where that lies, that citation and a quote, in fact, from that opinion is made at page 7 of our reply brief, in support of this motion. The prosecution has also made I think an interesting argument that a commander cannot ignore information presented to him, and they, in fact, have gone beyond that, and have suggested that a commander has an affirmative duty to collect information. We concede this is a very interesting question, but what we think the law and past cases teach us is that a commander clearly has a responsibility to read reports, and read information and acquaint himself with information that is before him and at his disposal. In fact, in the Hostage case, this very point arose, because there was a claim there that the commanding generals had not acquainted themselves with certain reports that had been prepared for their benefit and presented to them, and thus they lacked knowledge of certain of the crimes committed. The Hostage case Tribunal found that -- and I am quoting from the defence's motion regarding mens rea -- at page 13 the Tribunal stated that: "Want of knowledge of the contents of reports made to a commander is not a defence. Reports to commanding generals are made for their specific benefit. Any failure to acquaint themselves with the contents of such reports, or a failure to require additional reports where inadequacy appears on their face, constitutes a dereliction of duty." We do not dispute that. We think that wanton and immoral disregard could attach where there is a wanton and immoral disregard of information made available to the commander. But we do not think there is precedent, we do not think there is a foundation to go further and say there is an affirmative duty on the part of a commander to acquaint him or herself with everything occurring within their zone of command, down to the smallest blade of grass, and a failure to do that constitutes wanton and immoral disregard of their obligations sufficient to attach command responsibility and criminal liability for any misconduct that occurs within their zone of command. To create such an affirmative duty is to create the very strict liability standard that the prosecution has at least stated it does not embrace. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): And now I think that the arguments are completed. There has been a great deal of discussion, and exchange of documents has been carried out very professionally, and the Trial Chamber would like to congratulate the legal contribution of both of the parties. The arguments have pointed out this or that fact, and I believe that the Trial Chamber is now well informed of each of the parties' arguments. It is now noon. We have another hour to deal with the last preliminary motion about the defects in the form of the indictment in general terms. This is why the Trial Chamber decided that this motion would be the one to be dealt with last. That is the one on the defects in the form of the indictment, which, according to the defence, would have an effect on the entire presentation. I can now give you the floor again, Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. By this motion, we seek to dismiss the amended indictment because it is unduly vague and fails to give adequate notice of the charges to the accused. This motion, as the other motions, has been briefed in writing by both parties, and our specific views and the specific information we seek is set forth in the motion. I would like to summarise, though, that I think the gist, and the heart and soul, if you will, of our motion is, that we seek proper notice and some specificity with respect to the very conduct with which this accused is charged. The indictment, and amended indictment, do contain charges, allegations, regarding activities, alleged activities, of HVO forces or other armed individuals, but, if one looks for specific charges concerning my client, what you find is paragraphs 5.6 and 5.7 that, with respect to the universe of all the charges, he either ordered, instigated, planned, committed, knew of and failed to prevent, or learned of after the fact, and failed to punish subordinates. There is no act, specific act, with which he is charged. There is no specific omission with respect to which he is charged. There is no specific order with which he is charged having given. There is no specific report he is charged with having failed to read in wanton and immoral disregard of his obligations, and that is what we seek. What is it, the prosecution claimed, the accused did? We need to know that so we can respond and prepare adequately for trial. This issue has arisen in other cases. We cite those cases before this Tribunal, I mean in our brief, and in those other cases, the Trial Chamber, or Trial Chambers that addressed those matters, did find that there needed to be specific allegations of the conduct of the accused. It was not enough to simply say, "The accused was a commander, and things happened within the accused's zone of command". There should be some specific allegation with respect to the accused's conduct. Now, the prosecution has responded in part that, under the International Covenant on civil and political rights, notice of charges need not be in writing. They can, in fact, be oral, and they argue from that, that is at page 5 of their response, that they have given more than adequate notice to the accused. Well, they have not alleged the elements of the specific offences we believe with which they seek to charge the accused, and, as I said, they have not alleged any specifics regarding his conduct, and that is what we seek. It is inappropriate, we submit, at this late day, for the amended indictment not to serve as a final accusatory pleading, a pleading on which the court can rely, on which the defence can rely in order to understand the charges and measure the proof in the case against the charge. The indictment should not be a moving target. It should be a fixed statement of the charge at this late date for all the reasons set forth, and that is the basis on which we seek the ruling sought in the motion. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Prosecutor, your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr President, your Honours. In addressing ourself to the motion by the defendant on the vagueness of the indictment, the defence, as with Article 7.3 of the Statute, where he has attempted to re-write that Article by deleting the failure to punish provision, the defence, in this particular instance, likewise attempts to re-write the requirements of the prosecutor as set forth in Article 18.4 of the Statute as well as Rule 47, because, those rules, which are virtually a mirror image of each other concerning the substance therein, require the prosecutor to provide two things to the defence: a list of the charges and a concise factual statement in support thereof. What the defence would like to do under these circumstances is to substitute the word "concise" for "all facts", and that is simply not required under any reading of international law as set out by counsel in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and, likewise, the European Covenant on Human Rights. A review of the charges that are set forth in the indictment are more than adequate to identify the crime, and are more than adequate to give a factual statement, a concise factual statement in support of those crimes. What is the defence entitled to? Mr President, as you said in the Djukic matter, he is entitled to receive all his information, and certainly the prosecutor has fulfilled his obligation in that regard, and continues to fulfil her obligation in that regard, consistent with the literally thousands and thousands of pages that we have turned over pursuant to Rule 66A and pursuant to Rule 67A(i), because clearly no case presents all facts, no case presents all details in an indictment. That is simply not required. That is the function of the discovery process, and, clearly, that is the function of the Rules that have been set forth by the court requiring the prosecutor to turn over not only the material that is in support of the actual indictment, but also witness statements and a variety of other categories. Certainly, in the prosecutor's brief, we set forth what the requirements are concerning notice and facts as has been interpreted by the European Convention on Human Rights, and the case we cite as a case in point is Kaminski v Austria, where the court ruled that, when a particular defendant was told orally of the crimes and the brief factual statements in support thereof, the prosecution had complied with their requisite international law. Now certainly that is the bottom line, and we are not saying -- the prosecution's position, your Honours, is not that this particular case fits squarely into Kaminski v Austria. The prosecutor has gone far beyond the requirements of Kaminski v Austria and provided a plethora of information to defence counsel in conjunction with the charges set forth and the factual statements set forth in the indictment to enable counsel to know what the charges are, and to be able to formulate his defence. There is jurisprudence coming from this court, your Honour, Mr President, in the drafting of the Djukic case and also the Tadic case raised some issues defects in indictments. With regard to the Djukic case, quite clearly, there was a defendant in that case, General Djukic, was a logistics officer, a logistics officer who is charged with attacks on Sarajevo. Mr President, you and the Trial Chamber number 1 ruled that there was not a sufficient nexus between that particular General, who was a logistics officer and who was going on on the ground in Sarajevo. This case is entirely different, entirely different. This particular case charges General Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic, with ordering his troops, his men, men under his command, with killings, destruction, persecution, plundering, and the variety of crimes that are set forth in the indictment. There is no lack of link as we had in the Djukic case between a logistics officer and what was happening on the ground. This is a man that, the indictment charges, ordered his troops to commit various acts, and, if he did not order it, he knew about it and stood by and did nothing, and then he knew about it and failed to punish. So clearly the Djukic case, when you move into the particular facts involved, is inapposite. The other case that had a problem with the indictment is the Tadic case, where the prosecutor, early on in the history of this Tribunal, set forth a series of charges. In I believe it is paragraph 4 of that indictment, and the court was somewhat disturbed that a variety of conduct was set forth in paragraph 4, without a clear delineation of that conduct in facts thereof, taking the guidance of that decision, the prosecutor in this particular case did, in fact, delineate each and every item of conduct in separate paragraphs. If I can turn the court to Count 1, the persecution counted, the various methods that the prosecutor alleges that General Blaskic persecuted Bosnian Muslims in Central Bosnia are set forth in separate paragraphs, consistent with the guidance set forth by the Tadic court in its prior decision I believe in November of 1995. Clearly the defence is entitled to receive all necessary information, and the prosecutor is obliged to provide that information, and it has done so, and it continues to do so, but, as the Tadic court said, if, after reviewing all the supporting material which, of necessity, could not be included in an indictment, there are still problems with understanding what this case is about, what the particular defendant is charged with, the Tadic court invited the defence counsel in that particular case to file a bill of particulars for further clarification. Contrast the reply of defence counsel in this case. Defence counsel takes no such invitation. I believe he says on page 4 of his reply that it is not the obligation of the defence counsel to sift through the vast amounts of material that have been given over pursuant to Rule 66 and Rule 67 in order to understand what this case is about. I submit to your Honours that General Blaskic expects nothing less. That is a requirement of defence counsel in such a case. Based on that information, the information that is in the supporting material provided in both Rule 66 and Rule 67, and also the exculpatory material provided in Rule 68, which my colleague, Mr Harmon, addressed yesterday, gives a full understanding, not a concise understanding, a full understanding of the facts in support of this indictment. I do not intend, your Honours, to go into this case-by-case, but, if you look at the motion filed by the defence, the defence complains that there are no locations, no time periods, no victims, no property. Clearly, clearly, in a case of this nature, where hundreds of people are killed, some of them mutilated and burnt beyond recognition, counsel does not mean to ask this court to hold a requirement to identify each and every victim. Quite candidly at this juncture, based on some of the testimony that your court will hear during the course of this trial, it is literally impossible, because some of these British officers will come before this court and say the only thing that they saw were burnt remains, sometimes just parts of skulls, sometimes just parts of bodies. Who those skulls and bodies belonged to in some instances is in doubt. Nonetheless, timeframes and locations have been provided to the defence. Locations are provided within the municipalities and to the extent of which villages are involved, those are further explained in the supporting material that has been provided to the defence. Time periods have been involved. Of course, this is going to be a large block of time, because these are course of conduct crimes, the persecution conducted by General Blaskic in conjunction with other Bosnian Croats took place over the course of time. So consequently the bracket of time in which this crime is going to be committed is more than a day, a month or two months. As I mentioned before, the victims, in many instances those victims have been identified to the defence, and names are in the supporting material. Participants, participants, members of the HVO, soldiers under Blaskic's command, where possible, those particular individuals have been listed in and are described in the supporting material, when possible, when the witnesses knew who they were. The reality from that information as well, when we go into it in a little bit more detail, is that many of these individuals had faces painted, many of these individuals had disguises or masks on while this fighting was taking place, and many of these individuals came from other locations, were not from the area of Vitez, or the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak pocket. In those instances, identification was other than the fact that they were HVO soldiers, was not possible. Property destroyed and plundered, again the supporting material is replete with this information of all the property that has been destroyed, and the witnesses who identify the property that had been destroyed. The defence continues to argue about no information concerning the role of the defendant. Quite simply, the role of the defendant in this particular case is Blaskic was the commander of the troops that committed all these heinous crimes. His mens rea is set forth in paragraphs 5.6 and 5.7 under Article 7.1 and 7.3 of the indictment. What he did as a commander is referenced not only back to the law of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but what he actually did as a commander, giving orders, deploying troops, et cetera, and that is set forth in paragraphs 3 and 4 of the indictment. So there should be no question at this juncture as to what role this defendant played in commanding his troops under his direct command in Central Bosnia. His other arguments address some concerns, albeit without foundation, concerning how the particular statutes, or how particular crimes are established. One of those particular ones has to do with Counts 2, 3 and 11 where the prosecutor fails in the statement of the defence to include under Article 3 what portion of Article 3 has been violated by the defendant in Counts 2, 3 and 11. By way of referencing the court back, Counts 2, 3 and 11 charge violations of the laws or customs of war and they have to do with attacks on civilians and civilian objects. As the Tadic court recognised, while those are not one of the listed offences in Article 3, Article 3 is not an exclusive list. As the appellate court ruled, Article 3 is intended to be a residual cause, a catch-all clause, where no violation of international humanitarian law should pass by this court, and so we will view Article 3 as this residual clause which catches all violations of international humanitarian law which might not be absorbed in the grave breaches section under Article 2, or genocide, or crimes against humanity. In that particular Statute, we have charged violations, or crimes against civilians. Certainly, it is beyond any doubt that crimes against civilians and unlawful attacks on civilians are violations of the laws or customs of war, and absorbed into this residual clause, as described in paragraphs 91 and 92 of the appellate's jurisdictional decision. With regard to Count 10, there is a decision or a complaint that, referencing the particular charge of Article 2, we did not include "not justified by military necessity". If you look at that particular charge in Count 10, quite clearly the defence has notice of the particular crime that the defendant is being charged with. His last complaints turn to Counts 16 and 17, which have to do with failure to include, or the description of civilians being attacked, and if civilians are not attacked under those particular charges, then it is simply not a crime. I think a review of those two particular counts shows that not to be true. Certainly in Count 16, in the charging in the parentheses phrase, we can include the term "civilians" and in Count 17, which refers back to Common Article 3, Common Article 3 refers to persons taking no active part in hostilities, ergo they are encompassed within the particular language set forth in Common Article 3 and again, that gives notice to the defence of exactly what he is being charged with. In this particular case, a review of this particular case and the charges that are set forth completely notify the defendant of what he is being charged with. The concise statement of facts therewith is consistent with the requirements of this court as set forth in Article 18, and Rule 47. With regard to specifics and formulating the defence, there is no requirement by the prosecutor to give the defence, or to formulate the defence. It is the job and the requirement of the defence to go through the supporting material that has been provided to formulate how he is going to defend his client. Suffice it to say at this point, your Honours, that the information presented in this indictment more than adequately suffices under the Rules and Articles of this Tribunal, and the jurisdiction of this court, and Trial Chamber too. Thank you. JUDGE JORDA (in interpretation): Mr Hayman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. It appears Mr Kehoe sees only one purpose to an indictment, and that is notice. We believe, however, it is well-established in all systems that an indictment also serves as a final accusatory pleading. It must set forth the charges with some specificity so that the charges can be measured against the evidence, and that, we believe, has not been done. It is true we have been given discovery materials, and defence counsel -- it is their job to go through those materials, and we have, and we are, as they continue to be produced, despite the court's order that all such materials be produced by February 14th, we continue to get voluminous materials, and we are continuing to review them, but the fact that something is in the discovery may give us notice that the prosecution has potential evidence of that nature, and may seek to put it on at trial, it does not tell us what the charges are. Let me give you an example. In the most recent batch of materials that my colleague and I were given earlier this week in a meeting with the prosecution -- excuse me, in a batch of materials before the most recent batch, about two weeks ago, we were given voluminous statements. There are ten to twenty of them, concerning individuals who resided in the village of Stupni Do, and these individuals were attacked by armed aggressors, and misconduct, misdeeds, crimes apparently occurred. Now, Stupni Do is not in the indictment. There is no mention of this location in the indictment. We do not know if it is part of the charge or not. We know they have evidence concerning these attacks. They have given them to us, but we do not know if it is part of the charge or not. Now, we have asked the prosecutor that question, and asked him to make a representation to us, whether that is part of the charge or not. I am sure he will respond. He has agreed to respond. But, if he responds that it is part of the charge, that creates a situation where there is a charge that is, in our view, not in the amended indictment, and that is wrong, and that illustrates the danger, both to the defence and to the system of justice within which we are all operating, where an indictment does not have specifics, particularly as to the conduct of the accused, and the prosecutor can decide literally at the end of trial, after the evidence is in, what has he been able to show, and then he can argue what the charges were, that the relevant charges involved this conduct or this attack, or this order, or whatever, and not other conduct. So that is the nature of our request. Not only must an indictment serve a notice function; it must also serve as a final accusatory pleading laying down a marker, a benchmark for the court, for the defendant as well, of what the charge is. Now, Mr Kehoe, with great bravado, has stated this is a case in which the defendant ordered the attacks and the crimes set forth in the amended indictment. Fine, then let us name one.
